query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Mild controlled oxidation of multi‐element, near‐equiatomic nanoparticles forms a thin, passivating oxide layer at their high surface-to-volume interfaces that inhibits deleterious elemental segregation and phase decomposition under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized by physical or chemical methods that are initially in a homogeneous, near‐equiatomic solid-solution state with high surface area and no pre-formed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature treatment (e.g., 773–1173 K for catalytic operation and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use) to generate controlled, mild oxidation at the nanoparticle surfaces.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposures under atmospheres with controlled oxygen partial pressures, with one set treated in an inert (oxygen-free) atmosphere as the baseline and others in low to moderate oxygen environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, passivating oxide layer (potentially rich in elements such as Cr or other oxidizable components from the alloy) that forms on the nanoparticle surfaces.
generation.mechanism: The controlled formation of a surface oxide layer retards surface diffusion and elemental segregation by passivating the free surface, thus maintaining the solid-solution structure even under high operating temperatures. In contrast, absence of such passivation (as in an inert environment) leads to accelerated elemental rearrangements and phase decomposition.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles treated under a low, controlled oxygen partial pressure will exhibit enhanced structural and chemical stability (minimal segregation or phase decomposition) compared to those processed in an inert atmosphere, where higher rates of degradation via element diffusion and phase separation are expected.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles exposed to high-temperature conditions in an inert (oxygen-free) atmosphere, expected to show more pronounced elemental segregation and phase decomposition over time.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism is expected to be effective only for systems where constituent elements can form a sufficiently protective but not overly thick oxide layer; too high oxygen levels might lead to non-protective, thick oxide scales that could instead promote degradation, while systems lacking oxidizable elements may not form an adequate passivation layer.
generation.uncertainty: The exact thickness, composition, and protective effectiveness of the oxide layer in the nanoparticle regime remain uncertain due to the high surface-to-volume ratio and differences from bulk behavior; additionally, interactions at different temperature limits (773–1173 K vs 473–1923 K) may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a batch of multi-element, near‐equiatomic nanoparticles using a consistent fabrication method. Divide the batch into groups and subject them to high-temperature treatment under systematically varied oxygen partial pressures: one group in an inert atmosphere (baseline), one under a low oxygen partial pressure (to induce controlled mild oxidation), and one under a high oxygen partial pressure (to test for excessive oxidation). Monitor the structural evolution in situ using TEM and synchrotron XRD, and analyze surface chemistry with XPS or EDS to verify the formation and nature of the oxide layer.
measurements: In situ TEM imaging for real-time observation of morphological changes
Synchrotron XRD for phase identification and detection of segregation or precipitation
XPS/EDS for quantification of surface oxide composition and thickness
Weight change measurements (thermogravimetric analysis) to assess oxidation kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles treated under low oxygen partial pressure do not demonstrate improved structural and chemical stability (i.e., similar or increased levels of elemental segregation and phase decomposition compared to the inert atmosphere baseline), or if the controlled oxidation yields oxide layers that do not correlate with stabilization, the hypothesis is falsified.

First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

Corrosion behavior

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy [2] . prior_attempts: Numerous physical and chemical synthesis methods have been employed to produce these nanoparticles, but these approaches have not clarified the link between synthesis, structure, and resultant properties, leaving the underlying stability mechanisms inadequately understood.

decision.trend: Early work on multi‐element, near‐equiatomic alloys (e.g. in AlxCoCrFeNi systems) focused on how synthesis routes and subsequent high‐temperature or irradiation treatments lead to either phase stability or precipitation phenomena. Researchers used bulk processing methods (arc melting, spark plasma sintering, LPBF) and post‐processing treatments to reveal that controlled thermo‐mechanical history and atmosphere can govern the microstructure (including segregation, precipitation growth kinetics, and oxidation) and hence the resultant mechanical or catalytic properties. However, while these approaches have illuminated synthesis–structure–property links in bulk or micron‐sized samples, they have not resolved how such mechanisms translate to nanoparticles with vastly different surface-to-volume ratios.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved whether the thermodynamic and kinetic drivers that stabilize bulk high-entropy alloys under high-temperature service conditions similarly govern the behavior of near-equiatomic nanoparticles. In particular, the roles of surface segregation, controlled oxidation, and potential passivation in preserving both structural and chemical stability under catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) conditions—especially when noble-metal content is minimized—are not yet understood.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature treatment of synthesized multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles while performing in situ structural and chemical characterization (e.g., using in situ TEM or synchrotron XRD).
decision.why: This approach directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that a controlled, mild surface oxidation (or passivating oxide layer) stabilizes the nanoparticle structure by inhibiting detrimental segregation or phase decomposition under service conditions. It builds on the trend observed in bulk studies—where controlled atmospheres affect phase stability—and offers a clear controlled intervention to separate the influence of oxygen-induced surface effects from purely thermal or kinetic factors, thus fulfilling the identified research gap.
